vignette:
Juan is a 26-year-old man who stands at the threshold of his modest apartment, the air thick with the scent of dust and cleaning supplies. He works as a maid, a job that often has him scrubbing floors and dusting shelves in the homes of wealthy clients. The rhythm of his workday is punctuated by the sounds of vacuum cleaners and the chatter of house pets, all of which serve as a welcome distraction from the memories that lurk in the corners of his mind.

As Juan begins his shift, he methodically organizes his cleaning supplies, the familiar process offering a sense of control that feels elusive elsewhere in his life. But as he moves through the rooms, memories from his past creep in uninvited. The scent of bleach triggers a visceral reaction, recalling the sterile smell of the room where he was held captive. He feels the tightening in his chest—an unwelcome reminder of the panic that engulfed him during those harrowing days. 

It all began three years ago, when Juan was living in a different city. He had been outspoken against corruption in his neighborhood, a stance that initially garnered support from his community. But that support turned to a deafening silence when he was abducted one night on his way home from work. The men who took him were ruthless, and he endured relentless torture, both physical and psychological. Each blow and taunt buried deep within him, leaving scars that would not fade with time.

Now, in the present, he finds himself battling the weight of those memories and the feelings of isolation that come with them. He remembers the day he managed to escape—his heart pounding as he dashed through the streets, desperate to find safety. Yet even now, he feels trapped. The world outside his apartment sometimes seems too bright, too loud, and too full of life. He prefers the solitude of his small living space, where he can control the environment, even if it means facing the shadows of his past alone.

His colleagues at the cleaning service are friendly, often trying to engage him in conversation, but Juan struggles to connect. He laughs when they joke, but the laughter feels hollow. He feels like an outsider, watching life unfold around him from behind a glass wall. When they ask about his weekend plans, he offers vague responses, knowing that the truth would only invite pity or confusion.

At night, the memories surge like a tide, overwhelming him with their intensity. He often wakes in a cold sweat, the sensation of being restrained still echoing in his limbs. The nightmares are relentless, a looping film of terror that plays in vivid color. He wakes gasping for breath, heart racing, and for a few moments, he is unsure if he is still in that dark room or safe in his bed.

Despite the chaos in his mind, he finds solace in the mundane aspects of life. He begins to develop a routine, finding comfort in the predictability of his daily tasks. He cleans, meticulously polishing surfaces until they shine, as if by doing so, he can scrub away the dirt of his past. He listens to music on low volume, the melodies wrapping around him like a warm blanket. It’s his way of drowning out the echoes of his trauma, if only for a little while.

Yet, there are moments when he feels the weight of it all pressing in on him, moments when he stands frozen in the middle of a room, overwhelmed by the memories that flood his mind. He wants to scream, to cry, to let it out, but the walls of his apartment become a prison, and he keeps everything bottled inside, afraid of what might spill out.

Juan seeks solace in small things—his favorite series on television, a hot cup of coffee, the feel of a soft blanket wrapping around him as he curls up on the couch. But he knows that these moments of peace are fleeting. Each day, he navigates the delicate balance between his role as a dedicated worker and the turmoil that churns just beneath the surface. He is a survivor, but the journey is a lonely one.
